vignette: Three years ago, during a routine Tuesday night shift at the county emergency department, a pressurized steam pipe in the adjacent textile factory ruptures. Maya remembers the sound first-a concussive crack that vibrates through the linoleum, followed by the sudden collapse of the south wall. The blast wave throws her backward against the triage desk. When the dust settles, the waiting room sits in a tangled knot of shattered glass, twisted metal, and bodies suspended in the gray haze of pulverized concrete. She moves on instinct, tearing gauze from her kit, pressing dressings to arterial sprays, her voice steady as she directs colleagues toward the decontamination corridor. By dawn, she counts eleven bodies in the hallway. None wear the reflective vests of first responders. In the months that follow, Maya's apartment on the south side of the city grows quieter. She stops answering calls after eight, afraid the ringtone will mimic a pager. At the grocery store, the whine of automatic doors hikes her shoulders to her ears. She begins sleeping with the bedroom door locked and a kitchen knife within reach, telling her mother it is just a "new routine" for a single woman living alone. Her South Asian family, scattered across three time zones, notices the distance in her voice during Sunday prayers. She stops posting on social media. When a coworker mentions a "lucky break" after a shift, Maya feels a hot, metallic taste rise in her throat and excuses herself to the supply closet. She tells herself she is tired. She tells her family she is fine. The fine print is elsewhere. Now, at thirty-two, Maya's work as an emergency nurse becomes a series of calculated compromises. She requests day shifts, citing a preference for "administrative overlap," though she knows she is fleeing the night call lights that still clench her jaw. In the trauma bay, she avoids the resuscitation room with the malfunctioning fluorescent hum. When patients arrive with burns or blast injuries, her hands remember the weight of them before her mind catches up. She runs through mental checklists: airway, breathing, circulation. The numbers keep her from shaking. But the checklist is a dam, and she knows it is thinning. She double-checks exit routes, maps stairwell distances, and practices slow breathing until her pulse settles. Today, she sits across from me with her knees drawn together, one foot tapping a slow, uneven rhythm against the carpet. She describes the last week in measured phrases. A fire drill makes her drop a chart of vitals. She hasn't told her charge nurse. She lies awake until three in the morning, listening to the HVAC system kick on, convinced she hears the crackle of burning insulation. "I know the pipes are just old," she says, tracing the rim of her water glass. "But my body doesn't care about logic." When I ask how that sits with her, she looks past my shoulder at the window, where rain has begun to fall. "It sits in my ribs," she answers. "Like something waiting to break." Last month, she visits her aunt's house, where the smell of burning lentils in the kitchen sends her to the backyard for air. Her aunt does not understand why she cannot stay inside. Maya simply shakes her head, because explaining how a familiar scent can become a trigger requires a vocabulary she no longer trusts. At work, she navigates the hallway with practiced precision. She tells herself she is managing. She tells her family she is fine. But the symptoms do not ask for permission. They wait in the hum of lights, in the weight of a stethoscope, in the quiet hours when the city stops moving and her breath starts counting again.
